Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A needles/medical visual trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is clear trauma-related medical treatment, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in threat, memory, appraisals, or strategies. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal danger and intrusion rather than medical trauma cues, so this trigger appears clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid site of the event' is difficult to interpret coherently for ongoing or domestic partner abuse in this profile. If the abuse occurred in shared/home spaces, the profile would usually show corresponding location-specific triggers or avoidance themes; instead the threat items focus on general vigilance and home intrusion, making this item feel insufficiently anchored to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: The violence began during a summer of strained finances, when his partner’s temper curdled into calculated control. During the worst nights, his hands would pin Duy against the wall while the room grew heavy with deliberate silence. The assault left Duy with a fractured record of what happened; certain fragments, like the smell of spilled whiskey and the sound of a shattered picture frame, burned with terrifying clarity, while entire stretches of time remained completely blank. Unable to reconstruct the timeline, Duy found his mind constantly replaying the worst moments, making the physical pressure against his throat feel as though it were happening right now. Because he had convinced himself that the abuse occurred only because of the sort of person he was, he began to assume that any sudden silence or delayed response was a prelude to another attack. As the weeks turned into months, Duy’s hypervigilance solidified into a rigid survival routine. Walking into a vacant apartment to prep walls, he would automatically scan for exits before his tape roll even touched the drop cloth. When a supplier’s order took longer to arrive than promised, his chest would tighten, convinced that a catastrophe had already occurred. These mounting anxieties quickly hardened into avoidance habits. Duy began steering clear of anything that resembled his ex-partner’s belongings, and when a contractor moved too quickly toward him with a sample book, he would freeze completely, unable to speak or step back. The more he retreated into avoidance, the more his mind began to filter his environment for signs of pursuit. He would lie awake listening for the heavy footfalls that never came, and the exhaustion of constant scanning eventually convinced him that his own caution was proof of his inherent inadequacy. The loop tightened relentlessly over the following year. His tendency to avoid dreams left him perpetually sleep-deprived, which made his threat monitoring more frantic and his intrusive thoughts more frequent. Each avoided nightmare only served to preserve the unprocessed fragments of the event, which continued to bleed into his daily routine and reinforce his sense of worthlessness. When a client delayed giving feedback on a color swatch, Duy’s scanning for exits would intensify, and his memory of being pinned would surge with visceral immediacy. These unbidden recollections would then feed directly into his conviction that he was defective and out of place in the world. In turn, the belief that he was broken guaranteed that he would interpret neutral workplace interactions as threats, prompting him to scan for escape routes and freeze when confronted. This avoidance of confrontation and perpetrator cues meant he never processed the fear, allowing the threat system to remain permanently activated, which in turn fractured his recall further and cemented his negative self-beliefs. At twenty-four, Duy still worked as a painter, but the job had become an exercise in meticulous risk management rather than craft. He maintained his relationship with his girlfriend by rigidly controlling shared spaces, though the constant exit-checking and sudden stillness when she reached for his hand had begun to create distance. What finally brought him to seek help was a panic attack during a gallery opening, where the dim lighting and crowded sightlines made him collapse against a support column, certain he was being hunted. He was most afraid that the violence would follow him everywhere, but he hoped, if only for himself, to finally unlearn the belief that he deserved it.
